faq.a: Yes. Water molecules absorb red, orange and yellow light much more strongly than blue, so in deep water most of the red is soaked up and the light left over is blue.
asks: Why does everything look blue underwater?

faq.q: Is the sea blue because it reflects the sky?
faq.a: Partly. The surface does reflect the sky, which is why the sea looks grey under clouds. But deep water is blue on its own, because water absorbs red light and scatters blue back.
asks: Is the ocean blue because of the sky?

faq.q: Why is some sea water green?
faq.a: Green water usually has lots of phytoplankton, tiny floating plants whose green chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. Mud and sediment can make water brown.
asks: Why is the sea green in some places?

faq.q: Why does a glass of water look clear?
faq.a: Water's blue colour is very faint, so you only notice it through several metres. A glass holds far too little water to absorb much red light.

faq.q: How deep does sunlight reach in the ocean?
faq.a: Enough light for plants to grow reaches only about 200 metres down. Below about 1,000 metres the ocean is completely dark, except for animals that make their own light.

facts: Pure water absorbs red light much more strongly than blue light, which gives it a faint blue colour.
Sunlight is almost completely gone below about 1,000 metres in the ocean.
